sentences.text: This animal featured an elongated, narrow snout that closely resembled the beak of modern gharials.
Its dentition consisted of elongated teeth that curved sharply backward.
Unlike its living relatives, this creature lived in the sea within estuaries and shallow coastal zones.
Scientists primarily identified different species by examining variations in tooth shape, as these were the most common fossils preserved.
American paleontologist Joseph Leidy originally described the species Crocodylus antiquus in 1852 using material from Miocene deposits in Virginia.
The holotype for this initial description was a single tooth discovered in the Calvert Formation of Virginia.
Edward Drinker Cope later established the genus Thecachampsa in 1867, initially grouping two species based on teeth without a designated type species.
In 1882, Cope officially designated T. sericodon as the type species for the genus.
He also named the species T. sicaria in 1869, basing it on a jaw fragment and a dorsal vertebra.
The teeth of T. sicaria were lenticular in cross-section with sharp cutting edges, distinguishing them from other species.
Cope named T. fastigiata in 1870 as a reassignment of a species originally named by Leidy in 1852.
The genus was synonymized with Crocodylus in 1973 but is now considered a valid genus.
In 2001, A.C. Myrick synonymized Gavialosuchus americanus with T. antiqua.
A younger species was first described as Tomistoma americanus in 1915 from Florida, with remains found in formations across New Jersey, Maryland, Virginia, and North Carolina.
There are 39 recorded fossil occurrences of Thecachampsa in the Paleobiology Database.
Thecachampsa belongs to the parent group Gavialoidea.
It is classified within the class Reptilia.
Fossils of Thecachampsa range in age from the late Early Miocene to the early Pliocene.
Remains have been found in Florida, California, Baja California, and Costa Rica.
The time range for Thecachampsa is from the Thanetian to the Late Pleistocene, approximately 59.24 to 0.014 million years ago.
Some studies have placed North American forms within Gavialosuchus, but most analyses show a broad phylogenetic separation between these forms and Gavialosuchus eggenburgensis.
It is debated whether different tooth shapes represent distinct species or variations within a single species, as complete skulls showing these variations were previously referred to Gavialosuchus.
Most subsequent analyses reject the suggestion that T. americana and T. sericodon are the same species, citing clear differences between T. americana and T. antiqua.
